name: Affordability Crisis
title: Report: The Role of Housing in the Affordability Crisis | Tirzah Duren
description:
I’ve spent the past few months digging into the affordability crisis, trying to answer a fairly simple question: Why does life feel so much less affordable when many measures of economic well-being have actually improved?

What I found surprised me.

The data don’t tell a simple story of broad economic decline. In many areas, inflation-adjusted incomes and purchasing power have improved compared with prior generations.

Housing is the major exception.

Housing is one of the largest—and least flexible—expenses in a household budget. When housing costs rise, they can overwhelm improvements elsewhere and fundamentally change how people experience the economy.

And importantly, this isn’t primarily a story about the economy failing to produce enough income. It’s a story about the cost of housing being driven higher by supply constraints, restrictive zoning, regulatory barriers, and insufficient construction.

That distinction matters because many of the policies aimed at “affordability” focus on helping consumers absorb higher prices rather than addressing why those prices are so high in the first place.

If we want to make America more affordable, we need to focus on the underlying costs—not just subsidize them.
